article_title: "I Think You Have to Be a Fighter": Novice ESL Teachers' Descriptions of Advocacy for Emergent Bilinguals
citation: Garrone-Shufran, S. (2022). "I Think You Have to Be a Fighter": Novice ESL Teachers' Descriptions of Advocacy for Emergent Bilinguals. Teacher Education Quarterly, Summer 2022.
title: ESL teacher education should explicitly teach systemic inequities and pair novices with advocacy mentors
description: Based on the finding that participants' advocacy was tactical and lacked attention to the why of advocacy, the article recommends that ESL teacher education coursework include explicit study of how school and societal systems reinforce stereotypes and disadvantage emergent bilinguals, and that programs create intentional mentorship pairings with experienced teachers who act as strong advocates. Mentors who enact advocacy in all spheres would be most desirable.
requirements: Mentors who can model advocacy for novice teachers
Coursework explicitly addressing advocacy and systemic inequities
constraints: The author notes one course alone was not clearly shown to change participants' thoughts and actions in long-lasting ways
target_learners: novice ESL teachers
aspiring ESL teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: advocacy for emergent bilinguals
understanding systemic inequities affecting emergent bilinguals
examples: The author removed Suarez-Orozco et al. (2008) from the course and replaced it with three personal narratives by/about young adults who immigrated to the United States, to build empathy and awareness of systemic disadvantage
key_sources: Garrone-Shufran, S. (2022). "I Think You Have to Be a Fighter": Novice ESL Teachers' Descriptions of Advocacy for Emergent Bilinguals. Teacher Education Quarterly, Summer 2022. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1361502

article_title: The Influence of Principal Leadership on Classroom Instruction and Student Learning
citation: James Sebastian and Elaine Allensworth. (2012). The Influence of Principal Leadership on Classroom Instruction and Student Learning: A Study of Mediated Pathways to Learning. Educational Administration Quarterly, 48(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0013161X11436273
title: Framework of essential supports as mediating structure between leadership and student learning
description: The study organizes principal leadership effects through Bryk et al.'s framework of essential supports, in which "[the] framework of organizational supports for student learning starts with leadership as the driver for change" and leaders work across four domains: professional capacity of staff, learning climate, parent and community involvement, and ambitious instruction. The authors treat these domains as mediating variables between leadership and learning, distinguishing whole-school from within-school pathways.
requirements: Mediating school processes must be kept distinct from the leadership measures themselves so principal activities are separable from the processes they influence
constraints: The article limits its conception of leadership to the principal only, excluding distributed and shared leadership
target_learners: high school students in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: classroom instruction quality
student achievement (test gains and GPA)
examples: The authors modeled instructional leadership and teacher–principal trust as loading on a second-order principal leadership factor, with organizational factors as mediators in a multilevel SEM
key_sources: James Sebastian and Elaine Allensworth. (2012). The Influence of Principal Leadership on Classroom Instruction and Student Learning: A Study of Mediated Pathways to Learning. Educational Administration Quarterly, 48(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0013161X11436273

article_title: Education Savings Accounts and Accountability: A Landscape Analysis across States
citation: Berry, W. & Chait, R. (2024). Education savings accounts and accountability: A landscape analysis across states. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Landscape of 15 operating ESA programs across 13 states, varying by universal versus targeted eligibility and funding levels
description: Table 1 of the brief catalogs the ESA programs currently in operation, listing each state's program name, year enacted, type, and ESA amount as a percentage of per-pupil funding. Programs span 2011 (Arizona's Empowerment Scholarship Account) to 2023, and include universal programs open to all students and targeted programs serving students with disabilities, low-income students, or students in geographically defined areas. The brief reports "targeted ESAs are the most common, with nine states having targeted ESAs and four states having universal ESAs," with amounts ranging from 90% to 100% of per-pupil funding or fixed dollar amounts.
requirements: State statute and Education Commission of the States data as sources for the program inventory
constraints: Coverage limited to programs in operation at the time of the brief; four newly enacted 2024 programs had not yet begun operation
target_learners: K-12 students eligible for ESA funds, including students with disabilities and low-income students
target_learning_goals: Access to educational services of family choice, including private school tuition, tutoring, and specialized services
examples: Arizona's Empowerment Scholarship Account (2011, universal, 90%) and Mississippi's Equal Opportunity for Students With Student Needs Program (2015, targeted disability, $6,500)
key_sources: Berry, W. & Chait, R. (2024). Education savings accounts and accountability: A landscape analysis across states. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED663763

article_title: Evidence-Based Improvement: A Guide for States to Strengthen Their Frameworks and Supports Aligned to the Evidence Requirements of ESSA
citation: Hale, S., Dunn, L., Filby, N., Rice, J., & Van Houten, L. (2017). Evidence-based improvement: A guide for states to strengthen their frameworks and supports aligned to the evidence requirements of ESSA. San Francisco: WestEd. http://www.wested.org/resources/evidence-based-improvement-essa-guide-for-states
title: ESSA four-tier evidence hierarchy for intervention selection
description: The guide explains that "ESSA defines four levels of evidence" as elaborated in the U.S. Department of Education's September 2016 nonregulatory guidance. Strong evidence requires a statistically significant effect from at least one well-designed and well-implemented experimental study; moderate evidence rests on a quasi-experimental study; promising evidence rests on a correlational study with statistical controls for selection bias; and the lowest tier, "demonstrates a rationale," requires a rationale based on high-quality research findings or positive evaluation plus ongoing efforts to examine effects. This hierarchy is the evaluative standard used in the guide's evidence-review tools.
requirements: Users must assess both the quality of individual research studies and the body of evidence on an intervention
constraints: Some programs and funding streams allow all four levels; the Title I set-aside for low-performing schools does not allow use of the fourth level
target_learners: SEA and LEA staff selecting interventions for school improvement
target_learning_goals: Judging the strength of research evidence supporting candidate interventions
examples: Tool 5 (Intervention Evidence Review) has users assess an intervention's level of evidence against these ESSA definitions
key_sources: Hale, S., Dunn, L., Filby, N., Rice, J., & Van Houten, L. (2017). Evidence-based improvement: A guide for states to strengthen their frameworks and supports aligned to the evidence requirements of ESSA. San Francisco: WestEd. http://www.wested.org/resources/evidence-based-improvement-essa-guide-for-states

article_title: Community Schools Certification: An Approach for Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., Espinoza, D., & Oakes, J. (2025). Community schools certification: An approach for implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/220.412
title: Essentials for Community Schools Transformation framework: six key site-level practices supported by enabling conditions
description: The Community Schools Forward partnership, convening a national task force of leaders from 45 organizations, produced a definition, framework, theory of action, and indicators resource for community schools. The framework identifies six key site-level practices: "(1) expanded, enriched learning opportunities; (2) rigorous, community-connected classroom instruction; (3) a culture of belonging, safety, and care; (4) integrated systems of support; (5) powerful student and family engagement; and (6) collaborative leadership and shared power and voice." These practices are best implemented when there is a shared vision, trusting relationships, and data-informed, inclusive decision-making, supported by sustainable resources, shared governance structures, and continuous improvement infrastructure.
requirements: Implementation depends on shared vision and purpose, trusting relationships among school community members, and data-informed, inclusive decision-making.
constraints: While programs and services vary according to local context, the six key site-level practices are shared.
target_learners: K-12 students in community schools
target_learning_goals: student well-being and engagement
academic outcomes
school climate and belonging
examples: Figure 1 depicts the framework's enabling conditions, key practices, and supportive infrastructure, sourced from Community Schools Forward (2023).
key_sources: Germain, E., Maier, A., Espinoza, D., & Oakes, J. (2025). Community schools certification: An approach for implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/220.412

article_title: Community Schools in Los Angeles Unified: Transforming Teaching and Learning
citation: Klevan, S., Spitzer, N., Hernández, L., Rubinstein, C., & Swain, W. (2026). Community schools in Los Angeles Unified: Transforming teaching and learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/677.130
title: Essentials for Community School Transformation Framework
description: A framework developed by Community Schools Forward that organizes community school transformation around the traditional four pillars—integrated student supports, expanded learning time, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership—extended with two added core features. The report states it "extends the traditional four pillars of community schools—integrated student supports, expanded learning time, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership—by adding two core features: (1) a culture of belonging, safety, and care, and (2) rigorous, community-connected classroom instruction." LAUSD's CSI is explicitly aligned with this framework, and the added classroom-instruction feature motivates the report's focus on teaching and learning rather than services alone.
requirements: Implementation requires integrating whole child strategies across all aspects of schooling, not only service delivery
target_learners: K–12 students in community schools, particularly students from marginalized or disadvantaged backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement, engagement, and well-being through whole child community school transformation
examples: LAUSD's CSI is aligned with the framework, which guided its prioritization of welcoming classrooms, community-connected PBL, and Linked Learning integration
key_sources: Klevan, S., Spitzer, N., Hernández, L., Rubinstein, C., & Swain, W. (2026). Community schools in Los Angeles Unified: Transforming teaching and learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/677.130

article_title: How States Can Use American Rescue Plan Funding and Federal Grants to Support Teacher Diversity
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). How States Can Use American Rescue Plan Funding and Federal Grants to Support Teacher Diversity. EdTrust.org. https://edtrust.org
title: State ESSER spending on teacher diversity falls into three categories: educator preparation, recruitment, and retention
description: The Education Trust collected state-level data on ESSER fund use and organized it into a three-part framework: "Supporting educator preparation programs that attract and support candidates of color," developing or implementing programs to recruit teachers of color, and developing or implementing programs to retain teachers of color. The brief uses this taxonomy to present state promising practices in each category.
requirements: States must have ESSER set-aside funds available through early 2025 to establish or supplement such programming
constraints: ESSER funds are set to expire in early 2025, limiting the time horizon of these investments
target_learners: P-12 students of color
teacher candidates of color
target_learning_goals: Diversifying the teacher workforce to improve equitable outcomes for all students
examples: Georgia used $5 million for fees, books, and certification preparation in an alternative certification program; Maryland, Texas, Missouri, Nevada, Georgia, and Tennessee funded Grow Your Own programs; Colorado, Illinois, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, and Texas funded teacher residency programs
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2022). How States Can Use American Rescue Plan Funding and Federal Grants to Support Teacher Diversity. EdTrust.org. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED626513

article_title: ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming
citation: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703
title: Escalate collaborative scaffolds from minimally intrusive to directive only after lower-intensity interventions are exhausted
description: ProPACT's adaptive policy prioritizes minimal intervention and escalates support only when forecasted risk of breakdown increases. Its staged design follows the principle that "adaptive support principles that recommend escalating assistance only after lower-intensity interventions are exhausted, particularly under high cognitive load". Less intrusive tools (gaze cues, dialogue prompts, temporary Copilot activation) precede the most directive support, the task-based hint, which is reserved for sustained extreme mental-effort levels indicating cognitive strain or stagnation.
requirements: Real-time forecasts of collaboration states to identify when lower-intensity interventions have failed
constraints: The most directive support (task-based hint) is reserved for cases where both collaborators exhibit sustained extreme mental-effort levels
target_learners: Pair-programming dyads in undergraduate or master's programming education
target_learning_goals: Sustaining productive collaboration and cognitive balance without undermining learner autonomy
examples: ProPACT triggers a dialogue prompt when JME falls below threshold and reserves the task-based hint, which prompts selection of the current task and bug, for when less intrusive scaffolds fail
key_sources: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703

article_title: Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing
citation: Andres Karjus, Janika Leoste, Tiia Õun. (2026). Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing. arXiv:2607.16115 [cs.CY]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16115
title: Estonian reflective-writing AI-feedback corpus of 2988 homework triplets from 283 students
description: An anonymized text corpus from a first-year humanities course on digital skills and AI, autumn semester 2025, collected as ordinary coursework with an opt-out (none received). As printed, "It consists of 2988 homework (HW) triplets from 283 students", each triplet being a 300–350-word reflective essay, paragraph-length AI feedback from a self-selected chatbot using a shared course prompt, and a 1–2 sentence student appraisal. GPT-5.4-assisted annotation coded appraisal theme, helpfulness stance, reflection depth, and feedback specificity, validated against human coding.
requirements: Feedback was obtained using a uniform course prompt, slightly revised after HW4 to request more concrete essay-grounded feedback
constraints: Corpus cannot be published as open data; exact model versions, settings, account tiers, and system prompts were unobserved, and provider labels come from shared chat URLs
target_learners: first-year humanities bachelor students
target_learning_goals: reflective writing about lecture content
appraisal of AI-generated feedback
examples: ChatGPT was the most common tool (81% of parsed submissions), Gemini second (8%)
key_sources: Andres Karjus, Janika Leoste, Tiia Õun. (2026). Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing. arXiv:2607.16115 [cs.CY]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16115

article_title: The Power of Feedback
citation: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co
title: Diseño mixto con grabación en audio de tutorías de 6 docentes tutores de trabajo de grado
description: Elemento metodológico central de la tesis: un estudio con diseño mixto en el que el análisis cualitativo de los enunciados se categoriza y transforma en datos cuantitativos. La muestra, por conveniencia y no probabilística, correspondió a 6 docentes de una universidad privada de Bogotá; "el muestreo se realizó por conveniencia y es de carácter no probabilístico, la muestra de participantes correspondió a 6 docentes". La técnica de recolección fue "el registro del desarrollo de la tutoría mediante la grabación del audio durante el desarrollo de la tutoría".
requirements: Docentes con mínimo tres años de experiencia en tutoría, asignación de tutoría de trabajos de grado en el semestre, máximo dos estudiantes por trabajo, formación de maestría y presencia de ambos sexos
constraints: Muestreo por conveniencia no probabilístico en una sola facultad (Psicología) de una universidad privada de Bogotá
target_learners: Docentes universitarios tutores de trabajos de grado
target_learning_goals: Caracterización de la retroalimentación docente en tutoría
examples: El procedimiento se realizó en 6 fases: revisión de literatura, selección de docentes, consentimiento informado, recolección, preparación y análisis de la información
key_sources: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co

article_title: Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1
title: Common ground (shared understanding) as a necessary condition for collaborative problem solving
description: The editorial states that "fostering mutual understanding, which is variously labeled common knowledge, common ground, inter-subjectivity, and shared understanding" is one of the most important problems with computer support in collaborative settings. If participants do not agree on the framing and direction of problem solving, they cannot communicate effectively. Multiple studies in the issue, including Borge et al.'s, are said to corroborate that establishing and maintaining common ground is necessary for solving a problem collaboratively.
requirements: Participants must agree on the framing and direction of the problem solving to communicate effectively.
constraints: Not all conditions and tools lead to productive and efficient collaboration; characterizing the formal and intentional settings that evoke productive interactional processes is hard.
target_learners: collaborating students in computer-supported small groups
target_learning_goals: shared understanding of task and task-related processes
examples: Multi-touch table external representations support reasoning by making it visible and shared, thereby facilitating joint thinking.
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1

article_title: Relation Between the Essential Components of Reading and Reading Comprehension in Monolingual Spanish-Speaking Children: a Meta-analysis
citation: Baker, D.L., Alberto, P.C., Macaya, M.M., García, I., & Gutiérrez-Ortega, M. (2022). Relation Between the Essential Components of Reading and Reading Comprehension in Monolingual Spanish-Speaking Children: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09694-1
title: Essential components of reading framework applied to Spanish-speaking children's comprehension
description: The article organizes its synthesis around a framework of essential components of reading, which it enumerates as follows: "The essential components included phonological awareness, morphological awareness, alphabetic principle, fluency, vocabulary, and oral comprehension." The framework functions as the coding scheme for the meta-analysis: each component's relation to reading comprehension is estimated separately, allowing the review to compare which components are most studied and which show the largest relations in monolingual Spanish-speaking children.
requirements: Studies must measure one or more of the six essential components and a reading comprehension outcome in Spanish-speaking children to be codable within the framework.
constraints: The framework as applied covers monolingual Spanish-speaking children in studies published 2000–2021; the available text does not extend it to bilingual learners.
target_learners: Monolingual Spanish-speaking children learning to read in Spanish
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Foundational reading skills (decoding, fluency, vocabulary, oral language)
examples: The meta-analysis coded 33 studies against the six components and pooled 146 component–comprehension effect sizes with a random effects model using Fisher's z.
key_sources: Baker, D.L., Alberto, P.C., Macaya, M.M., García, I., & Gutiérrez-Ortega, M. (2022). Relation Between the Essential Components of Reading and Reading Comprehension in Monolingual Spanish-Speaking Children: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09694-1

article_title: The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2
title: Experience sampling method (ESM) for capturing macro-level emotion dynamics in language learning
description: ESM, also known as ecological momentary assessment, originated in psychiatry and collects real-time data on participants' behaviours, experiences and psychological states in natural environments. Participants are prompted "multiple times per day over a specified period ranging from days to weeks", via fixed, random, or event-contingent prompts on smartphones or wearable devices. The review proposes ESM to fill the gap of methodologies examining emotion dynamics from a macro, developmental perspective in language studies, illustrating a hypothetical two-week exam-period design with prompts after language activities plus contextual questions.
requirements: Mobile technologies such as smartphones or wearable devices to deliver prompts, and specialized statistical techniques handling multilevel intensive longitudinal data
constraints: Participant burden from intensive sampling may lead to fatigue or noncompliance over time
Repeated assessments may introduce reactivity, though studies have shown reactivity tends to be minimal and short-lived in ESM designs
target_learners: Second language learners in daily learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Tracking variability, stability and trajectories of emotions and their antecedents and consequences during language development
examples: The article sketches a hypothetical study prompting students after conversations, classes, essays, or reading to report emotions toward their most recent language use experience, alongside questions about topic complexity, conversational effort, and learning environment
key_sources: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2

article_title: Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach
citation: Goetz, T., Sticca, F., Pekrun, R., Murayama, K., & Elliot, A. J. (2016). Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach. Learning and Instruction, 41, 115-125. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.007
title: Experience sampling protocol with single-item state measures on handheld devices for classroom goal and emotion assessment
description: The study's measurement instrument is an experience sampling procedure in which students carried iPod Touch 4G devices running iDialog Pad software for ten school days, activating them at the start of 45-minute classes and completing a digital questionnaire at one random audible signal. State goals and emotions were assessed with single-item measures because multi-item scales could compromise state validity by prompting reflection and recall biases. Of 1779 initiated questionnaires, 1409 (79%) were completed, averaging 11.74 per student. ICC(2) reliability of aggregated state scores ranged from .734 to .921.
requirements: Single-item state measures to keep lesson interruption minimal and avoid recall bias; random signal timing within class; trait assessment administered after the state assessment to avoid influencing state reports
constraints: The restricted lesson time did not allow including more than three goals and six emotions; non-completion reasons included taking a test (51%) and other priority tasks (25%)
target_learners: 10th grade students in regular subject-matter classrooms
target_learning_goals: Assessing momentary achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions during authentic classroom activities
examples: State items included "My goal at this moment is to learn as much as possible" (mastery) and "At this moment I am experiencing [EMOTION]" on 5-point Likert scales
key_sources: Goetz, T., Sticca, F., Pekrun, R., Murayama, K., & Elliot, A. J. (2016). Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach. Learning and Instruction, 41, 115-125. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.007

article_title: From the Automated Assessment of Student Essay Content to Highly Informative Feedback: a Case Study
citation: Gombert, S., Fink, A., Giorgashvili, T., Jivet, I., Di Mitri, D., Yau, J., Frey, A., & Drachsler, H. (2024). From the Automated Assessment of Student Essay Content to Highly Informative Feedback: a Case Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00387-6
title: Four-component NLP pipeline for essay content scoring and feedback generation
description: A processing pipeline that takes learner-uploaded PDF essays and produces automated content feedback. The article describes "a pipeline composed of four components. These are 1) Preprocessing, 2) Segmentation, 3) Analytic scoring and 4) Feedback generation": text extraction and sentence tokenisation, sentence-level sliding-window classification into learning-tip sections, multilabel prediction of lecture-topic codes per segment against a ground truth table, and rule-triggered feedback texts displayed in a custom Moodle plugin. It was trained on manually labelled essays from a previous cohort and evaluated with a later cohort.
requirements: Manually labelled essays from a previous cohort as training data for both the segmentation and code-prediction steps
A ground truth table offered by the course instructors mapping correct concept assignments for each learning tip
constraints: Implemented for one particular task: German-language essays about ten learning tips in an introductory educational psychology lecture
target_learners: German-speaking university teacher students in an introductory educational psychology lecture
target_learning_goals: Connecting learning tips to lecture concepts such as working memory, metacognition and motivation through argumentative essay writing
examples: Students received feedback texts informing them of the quality of their essays and which lecture content they likely needed to revisit
key_sources: Gombert, S., Fink, A., Giorgashvili, T., Jivet, I., Di Mitri, D., Yau, J., Frey, A., & Drachsler, H. (2024). From the Automated Assessment of Student Essay Content to Highly Informative Feedback: a Case Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00387-6

article_title: Expanding conceptual evidence-building with the science of learning: integrating evidence weights, alignment estimates and iterative updates for educational innovations
citation: Natalia Kucirkova, Phil Vahey, David Patterson, David Dockterman. (2026). Expanding conceptual evidence-building with the science of learning: integrating evidence weights, alignment estimates and iterative updates for educational innovations. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10732-w
title: ESSA Tier IV evidence standard requiring a well-defined logic model and planned research
description: ESSA Tier IV is the lowest of four statutory evidence levels in the US Every Student Succeeds Act framework, relating to a research-informed rationale. Per the What Works Clearinghouse definition quoted in the article: "the product demonstrates a rationale if the study design follows a well-defined logic model and related research or evaluation is planned or underway". The article focuses on Tier IV for early-stage interventions, where empirical impact evidence may not yet exist, and observes that certification providers apply the guidance with considerable flexibility.
requirements: A well-defined logic model with related research or evaluation planned or underway
constraints: Certification providers differ widely in requirements: Digital Promise demands at least five empirical citations, an annotated bibliography, a qualitative study and a FERPA letter, while others demand only a logic model and rapid review
The article states there is currently no systematic methodology or detailed guidance for conducting the foundational research required for the lowest Tier
target_learners: US school districts and procurement teams
developers of educational materials
target_learning_goals: demonstrating a research-informed rationale for educational innovations
examples: The EduEvidence global certification system draws on the ESSA standards as one reference framework
key_sources: Natalia Kucirkova, Phil Vahey, David Patterson, David Dockterman. (2026). Expanding conceptual evidence-building with the science of learning: integrating evidence weights, alignment estimates and iterative updates for educational innovations. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10732-w

article_title: “Graphical” Jogthrough: expert based methodology for user interface evaluation, applied in the case of an educational simulation interface
citation: Stavros Demetriadis, Athanasios Karoulis, Andreas Pombortsis. (1999). “Graphical” Jogthrough: expert based methodology for user interface evaluation, applied in the case of an educational simulation interface. Computers and Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197391
title: Evaluate educational simulation interfaces by estimating the pace with which novice users become effective experts
description: When evaluating educational software interfaces, designers should attend not only to usability but to the pace at which novice users become effective experts with the interface. The article argues Graphical Jogthrough serves this purpose by providing “quantitative and qualitative data for formulating a useful (though rough in some aspects) estimation about the novice–becoming–expert pace” of end users.
requirements: Requires time-based evidence of user effectiveness, such as the Graphical Jogthrough graph of effective-user proportion versus time
constraints: The article states the estimation is rough in some aspects
target_learners: novice end users of educational software
target_learning_goals: becoming effective, expert users of an educational interface
examples: The Network Simulator evaluation, whose Graphical Jogthrough results informed the authors’ argument about the novice–becoming–expert pace
key_sources: Stavros Demetriadis, Athanasios Karoulis, Andreas Pombortsis. (1999). “Graphical” Jogthrough: expert based methodology for user interface evaluation, applied in the case of an educational simulation interface. Computers and Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197391

article_title: Teachers' emphasis on developing students' digital information and communication skills (TEDDICS): A new construct in 21st century education
citation: Siddiq F., Scherer R. & Tondeur J. (2015). Teachers’ Emphasis on Developing Students’ Digital Information and Communication Skills (TEDDICS): A New Construct in 21st Century Education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.10.006
title: Use ESEM with cross-loadings when measuring constructs whose factors plausibly overlap
description: The article argues that when construct factors are conceptually interwoven, ESEM provides "a better representation of the factorial structure than models without cross-loadings". Loosening the assumption of perfect item-factor links yields more robust measurement models that do not overestimate factor correlations. In this study ESEM outperformed CFA on all fit indices for TEDDICS.
requirements: Large samples and software supporting ESEM estimation (Mplus 7.2 was used)
constraints: CFA may remain adequate when perfect item-factor links genuinely hold
target_learners: teachers
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of multidimensional teaching constructs
examples: The study applied target rotation within ESEM, allowing cross-loadings approximating zero rather than fixing them at zero
key_sources: Siddiq F., Scherer R. & Tondeur J. (2015). Teachers’ Emphasis on Developing Students’ Digital Information and Communication Skills (TEDDICS): A New Construct in 21st Century Education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.10.006

article_title: Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report.
citation: Farris David P., Lebo Rachael A., Price Carrie. (2024). Designing a framework for curriculum building in systematic review competencies for librarians: a case report. Journal of the Medical Library Association : JMLA. https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2024.1930
title: Essential Searching Skills for Librarians on Systematic Review Teams course
description: A required Level I core course in the Medical Library Association's Systematic Review Services Specialization, developed and taught by the authors across eleven cohorts from 2022 to 2024, with approximately thirty registered participants per class. Each class used a Slack channel for communication and an open course site on Open Science Framework with readings, handouts, slides, and activity instructions. PubMed is the primary platform because it is "fully accessible without restriction to anyone with internet access and incorporates the MeSH database of controlled vocabulary." The course includes a five-question pre-test, four modules, a breakout-group search-building activity, and an identical post-test.
requirements: Delivered within the SRSS, which requires eight required core courses and four electives; participants are added to a Slack channel and given access to the OSF course site
constraints: The abbreviated three-concept activity was chosen over a full systematic review search because building a full search can take several weeks and requires input from an actual research team
target_learners: librarians of all searching skill levels earning the Systematic Review Services Specialization
target_learning_goals: comprehensive search strategy development, controlled vocabulary use, search peer review via PRESS, and search reporting via PRISMA-S
examples: The pilot class was held in person at the MLA Annual Meeting in New Orleans in May 2022, with subsequent online offerings and a final in-person offering in Portland, Oregon in May 2024

article_title: Difference among Levels of Inquiry: Process Skills Improvement at Senior High School in Indonesia
citation: Hardianti, T. & Kuswanto, H. (2017). Difference among Levels of Inquiry: Process Skills Improvement at Senior High School in Indonesia. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 119-130. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_8.pdf
title: Six-item essay test of science process skills on fluid statics (reliability 0.72)
description: The study's measurement instrument was an essay test administered before and after treatment to assess process skills related to fluid statics lessons. "The test consisted of six items with a coefficient of reliability estimated to be 0.72 in value." The process skill aspects observed were making observation, formulating hypotheses, interpreting data, drawing conclusions, and communicating results. Data were analyzed with SPSS 20.0 after checking normality and homogeneity.
requirements: Administered as pretest and posttest around the inquiry treatments
constraints: Content limited to fluid statics lessons
target_learners: Grade X senior high school students
target_learning_goals: measuring science process skills across five observed aspects
examples: Gain scores were computed as normalized gains (g) from pretest and posttest mean scores, with criteria of high (>0.7), middle (0.3–0.7), and low (<0.3)

title: Middle school science teachers should implement a variety of ESL strategies frequently, for at least 60% of instructional minutes
description: Based on their observation findings, the authors advocate focused instructional time engaging ESL strategies that promote academic language in science. They recommend that middle school science teachers "implement a variety of ESL instructional strategies frequently and for periods of at least 60% of their instructional minutes" to make content comprehensible and engaging for ELL students and economically-challenged English-speaking students placed in the same classrooms.

constraints: The recommendation is grounded in observed teacher implementation differences, not in student outcome data analyzed in this paper
target_learners: Middle grades English language learners and economically-challenged English-speaking students
target_learning_goals: Comprehensible, engaging science content and academic English language development
examples: Treatment teachers in MSSELL, who received ongoing professional learning, were observed using ESL strategies such as collaborative grouping (24%) and questioning (16%) of instructional time

title: Essential elements of educational games: shared elements plus education-specific elements
description: Citing the Arab Academy of E-learning (2010), the article holds that educational games, traditional or electronic, comprise essential elements: "Objective", "Rules", "Competition", "Challenge", "Imagination" and "Entertainment". Beyond these shared elements, educational games should incorporate adaptation to students' different learning types and previous knowledge, stimulants with instant response, and feedback with instant enhancement that motivates the learner to continue playing.
requirements: Entertainment should be equivalent to learning content
Games must have an obvious specific objective compatible with the player's goal
target_learners: primary school students
target_learning_goals: motivated learning of curriculum content through games

title: Escalating role of multimedia across teacher-training stages
description: The article describes a reusable design in which "The role of multimedia as a means of teaching is expanding at each subsequent stage". Multimedia shifts from visual presentation of material, to learning the technology of creating multimedia tools, to producing creative multimedia projects used in teaching practice. This distribution "allows us to achieve the goal of each stage of the methodology".

constraints: Described for Informatics teacher preparation

citation: Mercedes Rico García and Paula Ferreira da Silva. (2017). Acquisition of Language and Intercultural Competences in Tourism and Hospitality Studies through Active Experimentation in Second Life. Teaching English with Technology, 18(2), 69-92. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Four-unit ESP tourism course pairing B2 language content with intercultural dimensions and terminal role-play simulations
description: The course design divides a three-month course into four profession-oriented units, each following the same two-phase structure. As printed: "divided into 4 units, all related to the tourism sector and covering B2 speci fic language content in ESP, designed to prepare students for their internship in different areas, namely hotel receptionist, event planner, tourist guide and tourism consultant, and two intercultural dimensions". Each unit had 12 fifty-minute sessions: 8 for phase 1 steps and 4 for active experimentation in class or SL, ending in role-plays with clients or users from other cultures.

Clear task guidelines must be provided before SL sessions

target_learning_goals: B2 ESP language for hospitality professions
diversity awareness and multicultural acceptance
examples: Unit 1 role-play: dealing with Chinese, Arabic and African hotel clients; Unit 3: designing a tour for a multicultural group

Weekly projects covered topics such as parts of a computer, purchasing a computer, and implementation and management of LAN; the term project was designing a dictionary program fed by 2800 vocabulary items collected by eight groups. Co-operative learning techniques, peer and group coaching, individualized learning and activity-based learning were employed throughout.

constraints: Term project continued for three months and meetings took place in the library and the researchers' office

reading skills
translation abilities
self-instruction and co-operative learning

Term Project: Designing a dictionary program for the most frequently English terms in academic disciplines

citation: Abdul-Aziz Saleh Alsamani & Ayman Sabry Daif-Allah. (2016). Introducing Project-based Instruction in the Saudi ESP Classroom: A Study in Qassim University. English Language Teaching, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n1p51
title: Dudley-Evans and St John's Absolute and Variable characteristics of ESP
description: The article adopts Dudley-Evans and St John (1998)'s definition of ESP in terms of Absolute characteristics (meeting specific needs of the learner, using the methodology of the discipline it serves, relating content to particular disciplines, occupations and activities, and centering on the language, skills, discourse and genres appropriate to those activities) and Variable characteristics (possibly designed for specific disciplines, likely for adult learners at tertiary or professional level, and assuming some basic knowledge of the language system though usable with beginners). The authors state this definition is appropriate for the present study because it stresses permanently conducting learners' needs analysis.
requirements: Permanently conducting learners' needs analysis
constraints: The term ESP is more complicated than it seems and many new factors are being involved every now and then
target_learners: tertiary level EFL students in specific disciplines
target_learning_goals: English for specific purposes tailored to learners' disciplinary needs

title: Design ESP courses based on project work and extend project work to other fields and language skills
description: Based on the results of the present study, the researchers recommend designing ESP courses based on project work for other fields of study, extending project work in General English language courses, and utilizing project work to develop different language skills i.e. speaking, listening, reading, and writing. This recommendation follows the demonstrated vocabulary gains and reported motivational and cooperative benefits of the project-based ESP course.
requirements: Project work integrated into ESP instruction based on learners' needs analysis
constraints: Some project-based tasks may be beyond the knowledge of English instructors because such tasks are closely related to content subjects
target_learners: EFL students in ESP and General English courses at tertiary level
target_learning_goals: developing speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills through project work
examples: The study's project-based ESP course for computing students, which produced significant vocabulary gains and is the basis for the recommendation

article_title: The Search for an Effective Curricular Change Adoption in Foreign Language Education: A Meta-Synthesis
citation: Yedigöz-Kara, Z., & Bümen, N. T. (2022). The search for an effective curricular change adoption in foreign language education: A meta-synthesis. International Journal of Curriculum and Instructional Studies, 12(2), 337-366.
title: Ecological System Theory as a framework for curricular change implementation
description: The article uses Bronfenbrenner's Ecological System Theory as its organizing framework, explaining students' development through nested environmental layers: microsystem (classroom), mesosystem (school), exosystem (region/state), macrosystem (political/social/economic context), and chronosystem (time). The meta-synthesis maps hindering factors for curricular change implementation onto these levels, placing the student at the centre of implementation.
requirements: Curricular change must be analyzed by mapping factors onto the micro-, meso-, exo-, macro-, and chronosystem levels around students
constraints: Factors related to the exosystem level were not observed in the included studies
target_learners: K-12 EFL students
target_learning_goals: communicative language teaching implementation

citation: Demirkıran Engin Denizhan, Şener Tarık Emre, Perri Davide, de Oliveira Tiago Ribeiro, Caballero Juan Pablo, Osorio Luis, Kartalas Ioannis Goumas, Ramos Rodrigo, Castro Afonso Sousa, Reis Daniel Oliveira, Pereira Sergio, Dragos Laurian, Veneziano Domenico, Bozzini Giorgio, Somani Bhaskar, Liatsikos Evangelos. title: Stepwise ESU/SISE validation framework positioning face and content validity as Phase 0 evidence before CTA/Delphi and construct validity
description: The article organizes simulator development within the ESU/Standardisation in Surgical Education (SISE) framework as a stepwise evaluation program. The present study is framed as "a Phase 0 opportunistic expert appraisal of a prototype station delivered at a large-scale educational meeting", capturing early face and content validity evidence. Planned next steps include cognitive task analysis (CTA) and Delphi expert consensus to refine task breakdown, training requirements and assessment criteria, followed by construct validity testing with objective performance metrics and multi-center evaluation of skill transfer. Within this framework the simulator is classified as a Lower Urinary Tract Step 2 training tool for skill development and initial procedural comprehension.

constraints: At this point, it is not designed to serve as a platform for proficiency-based training or assessment

title: ESCO (European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations) framework as competency mapping tool
description: The ESCO framework, developed by the European Centre for the Development of Vocational Training, is the classification system the study adopted to structure and analyse the final transversal skills and competencies. title: Escape room learning is grounded in experiential and constructivist learning theory
description: The review situates educational ERs within experiential learning theory (including Kolb's, as applied in a renal-impairment ER for prelicensure nursing students) and constructivist learning theory, in which students "actively constructing knowledge through experience". It argues game-based learning within ERs fosters deeper cognitive engagement, and that ER scenarios such as diabetic ketoacidosis or aspiration pneumonia engage students in problem-solving that enhances understanding and retention of complex concepts.

constraints: Assessment of emotional and social competencies in traditional classroom settings remains challenging, which is the gap ERs are proposed to address

medical students
pharmacy and physiotherapy students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking and clinical reasoning
social and emotional competencies such as empathy and communication
domain-specific clinical knowledge
examples: An ER focused on renal impairment for prelicensure nursing students, based on Kolb's experiential learning theory, prepared students for clinical practice and boosted confidence

citation: Sarin Jyoti, Charan Gopal Singh, Bharti Richa, Sharma Sunali, Kaur Ekjot. (2025). Annals of African Medicine 24(3):540-548. https://doi.org/10.4103/aam.aam_66_25
title: Educational escape room structure: common goal, layered puzzle types, meta-puzzle finale, and debriefing
description: The review describes a reusable ER design pattern: every ER has "A common goal", requires "a series of cognitive, physical, and meta-puzzles" so every team member contributes, and puzzles are organized in "open, sequential, or path-based structures" of varying complexity. A meta-puzzle, typically the last challenge, requires players to integrate information from earlier challenges to unlock the final solution, and a debrief session by the gamemaster solidifies the learning.
requirements: a range of participant skills (searching, observation, correlation, memorization, reasoning, mathematics, reading, pattern recognition) to involve all players
a facilitator conducting a post-game debrief session
constraints: Educators must balance difficulty levels without making the experience too complex or too easy; time limits may increase stress for students needing more time
target_learners: healthcare students in nursing, medicine, pharmacy, and physiotherapy
target_learning_goals: problem-solving
teamwork
subject-matter knowledge aligned with puzzle content
examples: In the reviewed studies, 39 EERs used sequential puzzle pathways and 13 used open pathways leading to a final escape challenge

title: ESNPNSD: a web-based educational electronic system for developing non-practical nursing skills
description: The ESNPNSD is a web-based educational platform for nursing students to practise non-practical clinical competencies such as documentation, initial patient assessment, triage, and Kardex drug charting. It was built with a modular, layered architecture using the VUE.JS framework, MVC ASP.NET with C# on Dot Net 6, and MS SQL Server, with ASP.NET Identity providing two-step authentication. Students entered patient information after reviewing guide files, and professors monitored documents and gave feedback through the system.
requirements: Health informatics experts had to give satisfactory feedback and a passing score after technical validation of response time, scalability, and error rates before deployment proceeded
constraints: The study was conducted in the Iranian nursing education context, which the authors state may influence generalizability
target_learners: final-year nursing students in clinical internships
target_learning_goals: non-practical nursing skills including documentation, patient assessment, triage, and Kardex management
examples: The system was deployed to https://balini.esfrums.ac.ir/ for evaluation by four health informatics experts
Students uploaded information about a patient previously approved by their professor during the internship

title: The ESNPNSD is structured into three primary functional components
description: After consolidating overlapping items identified by health informatics experts, the final ESNPNSD system was organized into three primary components representing its key functionalities. The first, patient-related processes, includes "modules for primary assessment, triage, order checking, charting drugs in Kardex, and nursing report generation"; the second documents and shares useful experiences gained during patient care; and the third provides curated educational files and content. The pattern packages practice-oriented documentation tasks with experiential and resource components in a single platform.
requirements: Content items must be validated by expert panel review and consolidated to remove redundancy before structuring the components
constraints: Developed for the Iranian nursing education context, where the authors note such activities are still predominantly documented on paper
target_learners: final-year nursing students in clinical internships
target_learning_goals: non-practical nursing skill acquisition through structured practice and feedback
examples: Patient-related processes modules cover primary assessment, triage, order checking, Kardex drug charting, and nursing report generation

title: Electronic standardized patient (ESP)-based case-based VR simulation system for severe pelvic trauma with 3 ports, training and assessment modes, and emergency room, ICU, and operating room modules
description: A web-based digital simulation system integrating case-based learning with an electronic standardized patient: "we developed an electronic standardized patient (ESP) for severe pelvic trauma, capable of replicating both macroscopic changes, such as monitor display data, and microscopic changes, including alterations in blood circulation, organs, tissues, and cells." Students interact with the ESP as physicians in virtual emergency room, intensive care unit, and operating room scenarios; the system scores history taking, physical examination, and auxiliary examination and records inquiry durations. The platform has department administrator, course leader, and user ports, with training and assessment modes, running in browsers via a plug-in.
requirements: Students need a Windows 7 64-bit or higher PC meeting the printed hardware configuration (3.60 GHz Intel i5, 8 GB RAM, NVidia GTX 2060, 1920×1080) and must install the MengooLauncher plug-in
constraints: The ESP did not always accurately recognize the semantics and tone of inquiries, per the teacher interviews
target_learners: Fourth-year undergraduate medical students
First-year graduate medical students
target_learning_goals: Diagnosis and treatment sequencing for severe pelvic trauma
Emergency management of hemorrhagic shock
External fixation of pelvic fractures
Integration of basic and clinical medical knowledge
examples: In the pilot, 40 students completed training and assessment in the system, and 10 teachers were interviewed about its application

article_title: "MORAD ESCAPE", a novel research-based escape room approach for evaluating research competencies of health professions students.
citation: Mirshahi Arvin, Khanipour-Kencha Ali, Keyvanpour Sogol, Motlagh Maryam Karbasi. (2025). “MORAD ESCAPE”, a novel research-based escape room approach for evaluating research competencies of health professions students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06781-z
title: EscapED model: a six-component framework for designing educational escape rooms
description: The EscapED model, proposed by Clarke et al. in 2017, is a step-by-step framework for designing educational escape rooms and interactive game-based learning approaches for higher education students. The article states it "comprises six components relevant to escape room design: Participants, Objectives, Theme, Puzzles, Equipment, and Evaluation". The authors used it to structure the MORAD ESCAPE design, incorporating educational aspects as learning objectives and assessment criteria.
requirements: Design must address all six components: Participants, Objectives, Theme, Puzzles, Equipment, and Evaluation
constraints: The article applies it to escape room design in higher education contexts
target_learners: higher education students
health professions students
target_learning_goals: design of educational escape rooms as learning and assessment activities
examples: The research-based escape room in this study was designed according to these components and steps, with scenario development and instrument development as design-phase steps
